label: Agents author oversized, unfocused PRs (40,000-line loop output); split big prototypes into separate 1-3k-line PRs and use HTML diff walkthroughs to order changes.

cards.claim: Dark-factory claims from executives are mostly posturing; a principal-engineer example shows 30,000-line slop PRs where 90% AI-written claims are made.
cards.note: Dark-factory claims called posturing, with a 30,000-line slop PR anecdote.

cards.claim: Automated PRs must be small and digestible.
cards.note: Automated PRs must stay small enough to be merged.

cards.note: The 20,000-line Ralph PR was never merged; do not send huge autonomous PRs; rerun from specs.

label: Realistic gains for production work are 2-4x, not 10-100x, and reliability matters more than demos.

cards.claim: Aim for 2-4x incrementally and compound, not 10x-100x by discarding all engineering practice.
cards.note: Aim for 2-4x incrementally, not 10-100x.

cards.claim: His target for brownfield codebases is a 2-3x speed-up for staff and principal engineers, plus standardisation across a team, because many engineers each using AI differently produces chaos even if each is fast.
cards.note: 2-3x target for brownfield staff engineers plus team standardisation.

label: Target a sustainable 2-3x speedup at near-human quality, not 10x with slop that is thrown away; agent swarms and maximal token spend are the wrong bottleneck.

cards.claim: Aim for 2-4x incrementally and compound, not 10x-100x by discarding all engineering practice.
cards.note: Aim for 2-4x incrementally, not 10-100x.

cards.claim: Do not automate everything; take the 3x gains, fix the last mile only when it becomes the bottleneck, to avoid meta-tooling soup.
cards.note: Do not automate everything; be happy with ~10x leverage; fix last mile only if bottleneck.

cards.claim: Larger teams measure about 20 to 30 percent productivity gain from AI coding versus the 10x solo claim; his target is 2 to 3x on hard code.
cards.note: Teams measure 20-30% gain; his target 2-3x on hard code.

label: Safety through culture rather than enforcing hooks and gates worked at about 20 engineers, a counterweight to adding pre-commit or review gates.

cards.claim: On dropping pull requests: ownership culture (author owns it alone, no shared blame with reviewer) matters more than PR process; but he sends design docs to the CTO early because fixing before merge is cheaper.
cards.note: Ownership culture over PR process, while still sending design docs to the CTO early.

label: Name a specific reviewer or owner up front who reads the plan/design doc before code is written (author-opt-in review; design doc required before a maintainer engages; one owner drives, others read first).

cards.claim: On dropping pull requests: ownership culture (author owns it alone, no shared blame with reviewer) matters more than PR process; but he sends design docs to the CTO early because fixing before merge is cheaper.
cards.note: Ownership culture over PR process, while still sending design docs to the CTO early.

label: Linters cannot generally catch slop patterns (blanket try/catch, double casts) because the same code is sometimes correct; team rules can go in a prompt or linter but that is insufficient and no generic quality judge exists.

cards.claim: Screenshots and videos show correctness only; linters and cyclomatic-complexity limits block categories of slop, but nothing deterministic or prompted drives maintainability without a human in the loop.
cards.note: No deterministic tool or prompt drives maintainability without a human in the loop.

label: An architecture-review skill outputs a self-contained HTML report with before/after and a strength badge per candidate, then stops so the human chooses before any design is proposed.

cards.claim: Uses Matt Pocock's improve-codebase-architecture skill, sometimes accepting first fixes unseen, but its value comes from a human steering the refactor direction.
cards.note: Architecture-improvement skill is useful only with a human steering the refactor direction.

label: AI changes PR review pedagogy: say what is wrong and make the author work out why, since location hints just get pasted into Claude.

cards.claim: Good review comments probe and point to existing patterns; but pasting comments to an AI means the author learns nothing, so design-doc review becomes the place to coach prompting.
cards.note: Probing review comments; pasting them to an AI teaches nothing, so coach in design-doc review.

label: The design doc is the cheap place to steer: have the agent dump its understanding and patterns, then correct bad-pattern choices before any code exists; writing the design concept down also aligns teammates.

cards.claim: Good review comments probe and point to existing patterns; but pasting comments to an AI means the author learns nothing, so design-doc review becomes the place to coach prompting.
cards.note: Probing review comments; pasting them to an AI teaches nothing, so coach in design-doc review.

cards.claim: Because a design doc is a prompt, commenting on it teaches the author better prompting and may become as important as code review.
cards.note: A design doc is a prompt, so commenting on it teaches prompting.

cards.claim: Dex explains why design questions come before the plan: feedback early in the context is high leverage, whereas after a 1000-line plan (5-10 percent of context) most attention is on the model's own decisions and feedback is low leverage and degrades toward the dumb zone.
cards.note: Early design-question feedback is high leverage; after a 1000-line plan feedback degrades.

label: Flow control: exit a loop at start if its previous PR is still open, so work never stacks on unreviewed work (at most one PR open per loop).

cards.claim: Janitor bots hold a desired end state (refactors, lint-rule fixes, migrations) via small nightly PRs, at most one open per PR type tracked by labels, and no new run until the last is merged (kanban limit).
cards.note: Janitor bots with at most one open PR per type, no new run until the last is merged.

label: The research agent should receive only neutral current-state questions and never the ticket or intended change, so findings are not steered toward the planned solution.

cards.claim: Research is run in a session that does not know the ticket so it stays objective, then plan sessions (product requirements first if ambiguous, then design, then an ordering doc).
cards.note: Research session that does not know the ticket; adds the plan sequence of requirements, design and ordering.

cards.claim: Ticket becomes research questions; research runs in a fresh context given only the questions, so the research stays objective and carries no implementation intent (refinement of RPI).
cards.note: Ticket to questions; fresh context sees only questions.

label: Review in 100-200 line increments, peek after the first steps of a vertical slice and re-steer early; prefer five mini diffs to one 2,000-line change, and write long text in small edited increments.

cards.claim: Large work is broken into checkpointed chunks (about every 1,000 lines), sometimes as stacked PRs, to shrink the debug surface.
cards.note: Checkpoint about every 1,000 lines, sometimes as stacked PRs.

cards.claim: Re-steering early (design discussion, plan) beats fixing after the build, which cuts a six-hour review to 5 or 20 minutes.
cards.note: Re-steer early in design and plan rather than after the build.

cards.claim: Size phases to a verifiable chunk, checking in every 100-200 lines on hard work, because a 2,000-line result that is broken gives you no way to know how to change the prompt.
cards.note: Check in every 100-200 lines on hard work; a broken 2,000-line result gives no steering signal.

label: Default to the smartest model and generic mechanisms, and only do token pinching, context engineering or first-class integration on the high-use paths once usage or cost justifies the engineering.

cards.claim: Parent and subagent model pairings are chosen per task (big orchestrating small, or same model), he uses one model for nearly everything, and cross-provider orchestration needs the Codex CLI for now.
cards.note: Uses one model for nearly everything; pairings are chosen per task.

cards.claim: Do not automate everything; take the 3x gains, fix the last mile only when it becomes the bottleneck, to avoid meta-tooling soup.
cards.note: Do not automate everything; be happy with ~10x leverage; fix last mile only if bottleneck.

label: Be willing to throw away a wrong design or plan and rebuild or rewind rather than patching.

cards.claim: Incremental zoom-in planning (product, tech, steps) lets you discard output and return to an earlier level at any point.
cards.note: Zoom-in planning lets you discard output and return to an earlier level.

label: Research pays off: about 30 minutes documenting the codebase saves hours of thrashing, and research-backed plans put fixes in the right place.

cards.claim: A 10-20 minute async research step in a large repo gives the model 90-99% of needed context and misses are easy to find, which beats steering it interactively.
cards.note: A 10-20 minute async research step gives 90-99% of context.

label: Tooling catches functional failures but almost nothing reliable catches taste (design/maintainability) failures, the root cause of slop, so define what verifiers catch mechanically versus what stays on the owner's checklist.

cards.claim: Architectural taste comes from being bitten over years; models lack it, so humans must supply it, and juniors need mentorship by probing questions to build it.
cards.note: Architectural taste is not in the models, so humans must supply it.

label: Route by stage: strongest model for research, planning and checking/review, a smaller cheaper model for plan-guided implementation, escalating when it struggles (cheap writer, smart checker).

cards.claim: Fable 5.1 at xhigh was far more expensive and not impressive at solving the benchmark, so Dex sees it as a spec double-checker rather than a coder.
cards.note: Fable xhigh very expensive and not impressive on strict passes; Dex repositions it as a spec double-checker.

cards.claim: Dex's current use of Fable is as a checker of whether work abides by a spec, which is a verifier-role routing suggestion.
cards.note: Dex uses Fable as a spec/verifier role rather than a coder; same cheap-writer, smart-checker routing.

label: Benchmarks need to go beyond pass/fail: judge-model scoring against a golden patch plus a rule-based quality judge, and long-horizon multi-change benchmarks (e.g. 20 features then a 21st) to catch slop single-task benchmarks miss (SlopCodeBench).

cards.claim: The benchmark is about 196 checkpoints across 30-36 problems (he says 30 then 36 in the same talk), each checkpoint inheriting the previous code so the model builds on its own slop.
cards.note: Benchmark description: ~196 checkpoints, 3-8 per challenge, each inheriting prior code (30 vs 36 problems inconsistency).

cards.claim: A long-horizon benchmark (about 20 stacked feature requests, Harbor adapter) hands a later issue to a smaller model to measure the code quality the first model left behind.
cards.note: Long-horizon benchmark with ~20 stacked features then hand issue 21 to a smaller model.

label: Models are trained and rewarded on FAIL_TO_PASS/PASS_TO_PASS tests that never penalise design erosion or complexity, producing try/catch-everywhere and lazy casts, a model-training limit that harness engineering, tokens or user skill cannot fix.

cards.claim: Models lack maintainability intuition because RL makes them good at coding but nobody has worked out how to train for maintainability, which is partly an act of disobeying the instruction.
cards.note: Nobody has worked out how to RL for maintainability, so models are good at coding but not maintainability.

cards.claim: Coding benchmarks (SWE-bench style) and test-pass rewards give no penalty for maintainability, so models are not trained to avoid sloppy design; the verifier cannot be only tests.
cards.note: Test-pass rewards give no maintainability penalty; verifier cannot be only tests.

label: Optimise human wall-clock time and attention, not token cost: tokens are cheap, human time lost to an agent in the dumb zone costs 10x or more, so pipeline stages and spend on extra review/research passes.

cards.claim: Dex says token cost and agent time matter far less than long-term maintainability because maintainability compounds, a position that argues against optimising for cheap runs.
cards.note: Token cost and agent time matter less than long-term maintainability; users would pay about twice the tokens for cleaner code.

cards.claim: Dex's closing: if the user experience is a tight loop keep it fast and push heavy verification to background tasks; a rewritten workflow should ask what is synchronous, asynchronous or background (the guest's design-comment verifier does that).
cards.note: Keep tight loops fast and push heavy verification to background tasks.

label: Benchmark and effort numbers decay (silent server-side drift improved the baseline more than any skill pack in a month), so re-measure when a model ships and log model/harness versions.

cards.claim: The slop linters are partly stale (many from March), so newer models may have new slop patterns they do not catch and the detector set needs regular refresh.
cards.note: Slop linters are partly stale (many from March), so detectors need regular refresh and may miss new patterns.

label: Model and harness are coupled: models are post-trained on (and can be over-fitted to) their own harness, labs owning both have an edge, and a coding agent splits into model, inner harness (tool shapes/returns) and outer harness (orchestration).

cards.claim: Each model was run in its own default harness (Claude Code for Claude, Codex for GPT, OpenCode for GLM), so the comparison mixes model and harness effects.
cards.note: Each model ran in its own default harness, so model and harness effects are mixed in the comparison.

cards.claim: Dex says the genuinely new thing in harness engineering is RL-training a model on a specific tool set (apply-patch vs old-string/new-string), which is where product advantage lies, and that this does not apply to teams configuring a vendor harness.
cards.note: RL on a specific tool set is where harness advantage lies; vendor-harness configurers do not get it.

cards.claim: Dex distinguishes an inner harness (model plus tools) from an outer harness (even a bash while-true loop or orchestrator) and notes the dumbest outer loop (Ralph) still works well.
cards.note: Inner (model+tools) vs outer harness split; even a trivial outer loop pays.

label: Evaluate skills and harness changes by replaying a known-good plan or fixed task set with one variable changed, since plan, skills and environment are the only variables.

cards.claim: With a benchmark plus quality metrics you can compare many variants of a skill or linter (ten rather than three) by measuring the git diff after each variant, so skills and rules can be tested rather than assumed.
cards.note: With a benchmark plus quality metrics, many skill/linter variants can be measured by git diff, so skills are tested not assumed.

label: Whether to put periodic cleanup/refactor instructions in CLAUDE.md is contested: newer models may maintain code with explicit refactor instructions, but a human must know what to ask.

cards.claim: Models will refactor well when told to but do not volunteer centralising or refactoring as requirements change, so refactor steps must be explicitly asked for.
cards.note: Models refactor well when told but do not volunteer centralising or abstraction redefinition, so refactor steps must be asked for.

label: Harness engineering is optimising the integration points of the coding agent (commands, MCPs, skills, codebase organisation): the user-customised outer harness around the vendor's inner harness.

cards.claim: Dex defines harness engineering as engineering on top of the harness you are given (configuration surface of Claude Code: CLAUDE.md, skills, MCP) with a systems and context-engineering approach, not building a harness.
cards.note: Same definition: engineering the user-customised surface around a vendor harness, not building one.

cards.claim: Dex describes what a harness adds over a raw agent loop as extension points (CLAUDE.md loading, skill files, built-in MCP, context compression) that pull things from the environment into the system prompt or tools.
cards.note: Names the extension points (CLAUDE.md, skills, MCP, compression) that make up the integration surface.

cards.claim: Harness engineering is split into the inner harness (agent builder's) and the outer harness (feedback loops you engineer as part of the software factory).
cards.note: Inner harness by labs vs outer harness you engineer.

label: Harnesses work best when they mirror the tools the model was RL-trained on (simple flat tools, line-numbered reads); prefer built-in tool shapes and the stock harness over bespoke ones.

cards.claim: Dex says the genuinely new thing in harness engineering is RL-training a model on a specific tool set (apply-patch vs old-string/new-string), which is where product advantage lies, and that this does not apply to teams configuring a vendor harness.
cards.note: RL on a specific tool set is where harness advantage lies; vendor-harness configurers do not get it.

cards.claim: Dex says a model trained on one harness's tool format is poor in another, so tool formats are harness-specific and cannot be swapped freely.
cards.note: Tool formats trained on one harness degrade in another.

label: Stack outer loops that carry more process information than the inner agent loop (a supervisor of a few small structured-output prompts that classify done-ness and nudge, chained verifier agents).

cards.claim: Dex distinguishes an inner harness (model plus tools) from an outer harness (even a bash while-true loop or orchestrator) and notes the dumbest outer loop (Ralph) still works well.
cards.note: Inner (model+tools) vs outer harness split; even a trivial outer loop pays.

cards.claim: Dex's design has an inner Claude-Code loop per phase and an outer deterministic harness that checks the structured output (all questions answered) before moving to a different prompt built for the next phase.
cards.note: Inner Claude loop per phase with an outer deterministic harness checking structured output.

cards.claim: Dex shows a Ralph loop built in the SDK where a structured output decides whether the exit condition has been met, instead of a bare bash loop.
cards.note: Ralph loop in the SDK with a structured-output exit decision instead of a bare bash loop.

label: Ralph's lesson is that dumb things can work surprisingly well, so try everything and ask what the smart version would be; loop prompts commit with plain messages and no attribution.

cards.claim: Dex endorses wrapping deterministic or non-deterministic orchestration code around a good vendor harness as a high-leverage move, using Ralph as the proof that a trivial orchestration layer pays.
cards.note: Deterministic or non-deterministic code around a good harness; Ralph as proof.

cards.claim: Dex endorses Simon Willison's advice to keep trying dumb or futuristic things to keep your model-capability understanding current, and that flexibility beats locking in a workflow.
cards.note: Keep trying dumb or futuristic things to keep capability understanding current (Simon Willison).

label: Run each phase or loop iteration in its own fresh context window with one goal, the document carrying state; carve small units into independent windows.

cards.claim: Dex says the fundamental that made agents good is one goal per context window, with Claude Code continually recycling contexts.
cards.note: One goal per context window as the fundamental behind recycling contexts.

label: Building your own context engineering, prompts and workflows on top of the model beats waiting for the lab, because hand-tuned work extends the jagged frontier by 10-15% and survives model upgrades.

cards.claim: Dex's answer to the bitter lesson is surfing the models: new releases make prior code irrelevant but you can immediately do more context engineering and stay 5-10 percent ahead; the principles persist.
cards.note: Surfing the models: more context engineering on each new release; principles persist.

label: Code is disposable and value lives in specs and harness design, so for large mechanical refactors re-run the loop on fresh code rather than rebase or patch.

cards.claim: Dex argues that code written around a model is cheap to throw away if you have a decent eval, so the eval is the durable asset and the eval acts as the deterministic spec (auto research loop).
cards.note: Evals are the durable asset; code around the model is cheap to throw away.

cards.claim: The six-hour Ralph PR was never merged (a hundred merge conflicts two days later); his advice is not to send huge autonomous PRs, and Ralph output can simply be thrown away and rerun from the same specs.
cards.note: The 20,000-line Ralph PR was never merged; do not send huge autonomous PRs; rerun from specs.

label: Look at the actual traces and returned data rather than trusting summaries; understanding of agent work must be cheap enough to maintain.

cards.claim: Dex warns that the common failure in context, harness and eval-loop work is never looking at the data, and says do not spend a week automating what takes five seconds by hand.
cards.note: Failure is never looking at the returned data; do not automate what takes five seconds.

label: Prompts, tool shapes and skills tuned for one model do not transfer: running the same harness or Opus prompts on a differently trained model degrades results.

cards.claim: Dex says a model trained on one harness's tool format is poor in another, so tool formats are harness-specific and cannot be swapped freely.
cards.note: Tool formats trained on one harness degrade in another.

label: Exhaust the single agent loop and fix instructions before adding another orchestration layer; new orchestrators are about a hundred lines with no moat, so do not over-invest in them.

cards.claim: Co-guest Viv argues, and Dex does not dispute, that one should exhaust the single-loop stack (system prompt, tool design, context funnelling, skills) before adding another orchestration loop; Vaibhav counters that nested loops buy speed.
cards.note: Exhaust the single-loop stack before adding an orchestration loop; Vaibhav's nested-loop speed counterpoint.

label: Auto-research and tuning of prompts, models and effort need a good metric first, and testing should automate confidence with many sliceable dimensions per case rather than a single boolean.

cards.claim: Guest warns that auto-research outputs can overfit (60 enumerated if-else cases in the prompt, like benchmark cheating), so look at them yourself; Dex responds that production data and a human in the loop are needed.
cards.note: Adds the overfit failure of auto-research prompts (60 enumerated cases); needs production data and a human.

label: Evaluate by snapshotting outputs per case and eyeballing diffs between runs, and build eval fixtures from real or known-shape cases with a human in the loop rather than LLM-generated synthetic data.

cards.claim: Guest warns that auto-research outputs can overfit (60 enumerated if-else cases in the prompt, like benchmark cheating), so look at them yourself; Dex responds that production data and a human in the loop are needed.
cards.note: Adds the overfit failure of auto-research prompts (60 enumerated cases); needs production data and a human.

label: AI review agents and review bots are unproven against slop and mostly add noise (a model always finds something to say); AI reviewing AI is not the answer, and an extra same-model pass may be no better than a better builder prompt.

cards.claim: Dex states that every team should have an AI code review bot in the PR flow, calling it an objectively right take.
cards.note: Dex says every team needs an AI code review bot; family says review bots mostly add noise.

cards.claim: A pre-PR agent review step is just another workflow step, so AI review bots add little beyond a well-honed prompt.
cards.note: Pre-PR agent review adds little beyond a well-honed prompt.

label: Re-validate CLAUDE.md, skills and prompts at every model release, because harness pieces expire as models improve.

cards.claim: Dex endorses designing so capabilities are easy to delete when the model improves and being careful what you expose as a product substrate, to avoid accumulating tech debt.
cards.note: Design capabilities to be easy to delete as models improve; harness pieces expire.

label: Human on the loop (designing and steering the loop, stopping at chosen points) is better than human in the loop.

cards.claim: Dex agrees a human in the loop inside the outer loop is a good way to inject intelligence, and warns against over-engineering automation of small tasks.
cards.note: Human inside the outer loop as intelligence injection; nuanced against on-the-loop framing.

label: Every spec or PRD defines a measurable success signal or post-ship lever so a later agent can check whether it worked (or records that none fits).

cards.claim: Dex tells (as an analogy from Google/Facebook deploys) that an agent loop needs a prod metric and gradual rollout with a human watching at release, since without prod data you overfit to the wrong thing.
cards.note: Every feature has a metric and gradual rollout watched by a human; prod data prevents overfitting.

label: Break one large prompt or skill into several small focused workflows and use code, not prompts, for control flow; there is no magic prompt, and the 12-factor 'no monolith' advice was ignored by their own monolithic prompt.

cards.claim: Dex says control flow written as prompt instructions (control flow via prompt) is a mistake: if you know the order, use a script, as a make-task agent needed two hours of added instructions where a 90-second bash script sufficed.
cards.note: Control flow in prompts is a mistake; 2 hours of prompt vs 90-second script anecdote.

cards.claim: Dex's headline takeaway: do not use prompts for control flow; start broad and robust, learn actual inputs, add more deterministic happy paths and keep a fully agentic escape hatch.
cards.note: Headline takeaway: do not use prompts for control flow; keep an agentic escape hatch.

cards.claim: The create-plan prompt had about 50 instructions; he now splits planning into multiple steps wrapped in deterministic code, applying 12-factor-agents advice not to use prompts for control flow.
cards.note: Create-plan prompt of about 50 instructions split into steps wrapped in code; control flow in code, not prompts.

label: Sequence and control flow belong in code or separate workflow steps, not in a monolithic prompt or magic words; a tool that needs magic words is broken.

cards.claim: Dex says control flow written as prompt instructions (control flow via prompt) is a mistake: if you know the order, use a script, as a make-task agent needed two hours of added instructions where a 90-second bash script sufficed.
cards.note: Control flow in prompts is a mistake; 2 hours of prompt vs 90-second script anecdote.

cards.claim: Dex's headline takeaway: do not use prompts for control flow; start broad and robust, learn actual inputs, add more deterministic happy paths and keep a fully agentic escape hatch.
cards.note: Headline takeaway: do not use prompts for control flow; keep an agentic escape hatch.

cards.claim: Where the workflow is known, make steps deterministic code with small LLM steps inside rather than steering the sequence with prompt text.
cards.note: Deterministic steps with small LLM steps, not prompts for control flow.

cards.claim: A single create-plan prompt carrying design, structure and plan instructions got steps skipped, so he split it into separate prompts and context windows (a change from the one-prompt RPI planning step).
cards.note: Same split of one long create-plan prompt; skipped design/structure steps.

label: Models skip interactive steps of a prompt even when instructed (even Opus 4.1/4.5), so the key orders must be reinforced in the user message, and novices will not notice the skip.

cards.claim: Dex reports that with the create-plan prompt customers rushed and the model skipped the early design-question and outline phases, which are what make the plan good; without them the plan is little better than 'go write the code'.
cards.note: Customers rushed create-plan and the model skipped design-question and outline phases.

label: A monolithic multi-step prompt of 50-85 instructions had steps skipped about half the time; splitting it into prompts under 40 instructions each fixed the skipping.

cards.claim: Dex reports that with the create-plan prompt customers rushed and the model skipped the early design-question and outline phases, which are what make the plan good; without them the plan is little better than 'go write the code'.
cards.note: Customers rushed create-plan and the model skipped design-question and outline phases.

cards.claim: A single create-plan prompt carrying design, structure and plan instructions got steps skipped, so he split it into separate prompts and context windows (a change from the one-prompt RPI planning step).
cards.note: Same split of one long create-plan prompt; skipped design/structure steps.

cards.claim: The create-plan prompt had about 50 instructions; he now splits planning into multiple steps wrapped in deterministic code, applying 12-factor-agents advice not to use prompts for control flow.
cards.note: Create-plan prompt of about 50 instructions split into steps wrapped in code; control flow in code, not prompts.

label: Frontier models follow about 150-200 instructions reliably, the Claude Code system prompt already uses ~50, and quality drops uniformly as the count grows, so count instructions not lines.

cards.claim: Dex cites Kyle's study that frontier LLMs follow roughly 150-200 instructions reliably (as of about mid-2026 minus six months, probably higher now) and says the create-plan prompt holds over a hundred, repeated and in caps.
cards.note: Restates 150-200 instruction figure, recalled as 6-7 months old and probably higher now; create-plan prompt holds over a hundred.

label: The instruction-count versus accuracy research behind the trim targets uses models over six months old and may not hold for current models.

cards.claim: Dex cites Kyle's study that frontier LLMs follow roughly 150-200 instructions reliably (as of about mid-2026 minus six months, probably higher now) and says the create-plan prompt holds over a hundred, repeated and in caps.
cards.note: Restates 150-200 instruction figure, recalled as 6-7 months old and probably higher now; create-plan prompt holds over a hundred.

label: Prompt emphasis (shouting, capitals) is model-specific and can detune some models.

cards.claim: Dex says emphatic caps (must, critical, never) do not buy compliance because the model can attend to only so many instructions; split the prompt into separate smaller workflows instead.
cards.note: Capitalised emphasis does not buy compliance; split the prompt instead.

label: Make architecture and design decisions early in a short window, where reasoning is best and not yet biased by written code; later discovery costs more.

cards.claim: Dex explains why design questions come before the plan: feedback early in the context is high leverage, whereas after a 1000-line plan (5-10 percent of context) most attention is on the model's own decisions and feedback is low leverage and degrades toward the dumb zone.
cards.note: Early design-question feedback is high leverage; after a 1000-line plan feedback degrades.

label: When implementation reveals a plan or spec error, fix the plan upstream and rerun implementation rather than patching code; editing a plan in flight remains an open problem.

cards.claim: Editing a plan after feedback in the same context yields inconsistent partial application; when a fast one-shot plan is not ~95 percent right, delete it and restart down the interactive path rather than re-steer.
cards.note: Editing a plan in-context applies feedback inconsistently; restart if one-shot plan is not ~95% right.

cards.claim: Try the one-shot version first; if the result is poor, rewind to the design discussion and lower the autonomy level rather than start over.
cards.note: Rewind to design discussion and lower autonomy instead of restarting.

label: If an implementation is ~5% wrong steer it; if ~30% wrong, restart from the ticket because tokens are cheap relative to re-steering.

cards.claim: Editing a plan after feedback in the same context yields inconsistent partial application; when a fast one-shot plan is not ~95 percent right, delete it and restart down the interactive path rather than re-steer.
cards.note: Editing a plan in-context applies feedback inconsistently; restart if one-shot plan is not ~95% right.

cards.claim: Try the one-shot version first; if the result is poor, rewind to the design discussion and lower the autonomy level rather than start over.
cards.note: Rewind to design discussion and lower autonomy instead of restarting.

label: Design the whole workflow around frequent intentional compaction: each step ends in a compacted artifact and the next starts in a fresh small window.

cards.claim: Dex's structured-planning SDK splits one big prompt into design, structure and plan agents with schema-typed outputs and deterministic code between phases, forcing intentional compaction at phase boundaries instead of relying on users to know when to start fresh.
cards.note: SDK splits design/structure/plan agents with schema outputs, forcing compaction at phase boundaries.

cards.claim: Each stage compacts context into a document with a specific output format, and later stages deterministically allocate the existing docs into the next context window.

cards.note: Dex expects tool search to make large MCP sets less of a context problem (untested).

label: Loading many MCP servers/tool definitions eats the context budget (measured about 5.7k tokens for one MCP), so tool surface should be chosen per need.

label: Make context use visible (a /context breakdown, an always-visible meter, model-aware warnings, tracked token counts) so budget decisions use a number.

cards.claim: A Ralph tool should chart context used per iteration and per component so you see that loops always reach 60% and shrink the task; he and Matt note observability here is currently poor.
cards.note: Proposes charting context used per iteration and component in a Ralph tool.

label: Frame an agent as a control loop (desired state, current state, one action, re-read) borrowed from Kubernetes controllers.

cards.claim: Ralph is framed as a Kubernetes-style control loop: read specs (desired state) and source (current state), implement one thing, repeat, so every iteration starts in the smart zone.
cards.note: Ralph as Kubernetes-style control loop, every iteration in the smart zone.

label: Ralph is deterministic context allocation, like malloc: fixed budgets for system prompt and state, re-derived from specs and repo each iteration (control loop).

cards.claim: Ralph is framed as a Kubernetes-style control loop: read specs (desired state) and source (current state), implement one thing, repeat, so every iteration starts in the smart zone.
cards.note: Ralph as Kubernetes-style control loop, every iteration in the smart zone.

label: Size each phase to fit one context window, leaving headroom for tests and commit/PR steps, and plan so errors are recoverable within a session.

cards.claim: Size a task so edit, test, fix, retest and commit all fit in as little context as possible, but not so small that a signature change cannot pass tests without touching other files.
cards.note: Size a task so edit, test, fix, commit fit in minimal context but not too small.

label: Ran a Ralph loop on a refactoring experiment and drew lessons about incremental improvement.

cards.claim: Worked Ralph example: a 30-minute Claude interview plus 30 minutes with a front-end engineer produced about 25-27 React style rules, then a Ralph loop on a cloud VM refactored toward them for about six hours.
cards.note: Adds the measured worked Ralph example: style-guide interview, 6 hours, 20 commits, 20,000-line PR.

label: Bound every unattended loop with iteration, time or turn caps and an external stop, because a left-running loop invents new work and 'overbakes', moving to a needs-human state after ~4-5 respawns.

cards.claim: Ralph can be over-baked: left running past the point of done, the model invents extra work (for example post-quantum cryptography in a toy language), analogous to rolling back an overfit model to a checkpoint.
cards.note: Ralph left running too long invents extra work (overbaking).

label: Ralph loops are valuable for the context-engineering lessons, not as a production technique.

cards.claim: Ralph is valuable mainly as a lesson in how context windows work; engineers should learn the theory rather than just install the plugin; a chained spec-to-spec-to-code Ralph pipeline he tried did not produce a product he liked.
cards.note: Ralph valuable as a lesson in context windows, not final answer for production software; adds one failed chained-loop experiment.

label: Recurring CI agents carry queue controls: a no-op guard (exit if an open agent PR exists), a concurrency group, a repo memory file in each prompt, a no-commit-no-PR guard, an actor gate on comment triggers.

cards.claim: His production-safe version of Ralph is a nightly cron or GitHub Action running three iterations against a spec of the desired architecture, producing small incremental PRs he need not merge.
cards.note: Production-safe Ralph as nightly cron running three iterations to produce small PRs.

label: Put a human triage queue between public issues and the tickets a background agent can read, so outsiders cannot inject the agent or steer product work.

cards.claim: Never feed community-submitted issues to an agent running with skipped permissions; his team's Linear queue route requires a human to check for hidden prompts in HTML or markdown comments before the model sees anything.
cards.note: Community issues are untrusted input; human checks for hidden prompts before the agent sees them.

label: The implementation skill is an orchestrator launching one implementer sub-agent per plan phase with a one-line prompt pointing at the plan, re-running checks itself, waiting for human sign-off, and resuming from the first unchecked box.

cards.claim: For hard problems, work stays human-in-the-loop; the CodeLayer plan prompt uses a parent agent that runs each task in a sub-agent, checks the work, commits and moves to the next phase.
cards.note: CodeLayer plan prompt uses a parent agent running each task in a sub-agent; hard problems stay human-in-the-loop.

label: For black-box dependencies write small runnable learning tests/proofs (kept out of the normal suite, re-run manually on upgrades, agent can author new ones from examples) instead of trusting docs or model assertions, including absence reports from search subagents.

cards.claim: Write 'learning tests' that assert the real contract of an external system (his example is the closed-source Claude Agent SDK) before building on it; rerun them when behaviour seems to change, as when session-ID behaviour changed.
cards.note: Learning tests on the closed-source Agent SDK; rerun caught a session-ID contract change.

label: Default to one phase per run with a mandatory pause after automated checks and a fixed 'Ready for Manual Verification' message; manual boxes are ticked only after user confirmation.

cards.claim: Write plans that work both ways: fire-and-forget through all phases, or check in after every phase when the work is delicate; and the key new skill is knowing how the model will know its output matches human intent.
cards.note: Dual-purpose plans (fire-and-forget or per-phase check-ins); skill is knowing how the model verifies intent.

label: Design the verification mechanism before the implementation: the best agent engineers spent days designing the checks, then ran the loop unattended for ~2 days and got tens of thousands of working lines.

cards.claim: Write plans that work both ways: fire-and-forget through all phases, or check in after every phase when the work is delicate; and the key new skill is knowing how the model will know its output matches human intent.
cards.note: Dual-purpose plans (fire-and-forget or per-phase check-ins); skill is knowing how the model verifies intent.

label: Adoption came through open-sourced prompts that other products copied, and the product was rebuilt from about 60k to 35k lines.

cards.claim: In six weeks he rebuilt CodeLayer from scratch around more guided workflows after rolling it out to customers.
cards.note: CodeLayer rebuilt in six weeks around more guided workflows after customer rollout.

label: Give each parallel agent its own worktree stack and never stop another worktree's stack.

cards.claim: Two agents in one checkout step on each other (for example contending on the Cargo lock, slowing both builds), so parallel agents need separate working directories.
cards.note: Two agents in one checkout contend (Cargo lock); separate working directories.

label: Make a worktree's start state reproducible: start from a pinned remote ref, copy local settings and env files, run a setup command, and show setup status to the agent.

cards.claim: A worktree is only usable if one setup script (for example make setup) installs dependencies and copies untracked files such as .env and .claude; the repo defines setup, a generic create-worktree script runs it, and a failed setup auto-cleans the worktree.
cards.note: One make-setup script run by a generic create-worktree script with auto-clean on failure.

cards.claim: On creating a worktree, copy the git-ignored settings.local.json (personal permissions) by copying the whole .claude directory, since only committed files arrive in a new worktree.
cards.note: Copy the whole .claude directory so git-ignored local settings reach the new worktree.

label: Parallelism is capped by human design and review capacity (2-3 parallel runs; agent teams create stitching work), so fan out only after a good plan.

cards.claim: A merge-watcher agent looping every 60 seconds can merge worker branches (with pre-commit tests mandatory in agent-only worktrees), but more automation means more deviation; his multi-claude manager-agent tool predates sub-agents and he warns not to over-parallelise.
cards.note: Merge-watcher loop demo; more automation means more deviation; warns against over-parallelising.

label: Run each task in its own worktree with a predictable branch name, decide worktree timing after plan review, and exclude tool state from git.

cards.claim: Fix a worktree convention up front (all under ~/worktree/repo/branch) and name branches person/feature (sometimes with a date); worktrees should be cleaned up after merge like local branches.
cards.note: Fixed worktree path convention, person/feature branch names, cleanup after merge.

cards.claim: Do research and planning on main, keep the markdown docs outside the code worktree (separate repo or vault, not merge-sensitive) and create the worktree only once the plan is good; overusing worktrees creates chaos.
cards.note: Research and plan on main with docs outside the worktree; create the worktree after plan review.

label: Adopt incrementally and treat early trials as experiments: hill-climb from the current process, pilot first, dry-run a new routine before trusting it, and expect to revise views.

cards.claim: Adopt a new practice as a two-week time-bounded experiment, then re-evaluate; the worst case is perhaps 20-30% slower for two weeks.
cards.note: Adopt a practice as a two-week time-bounded experiment.

label: Use a multi-stage pipeline (questions, research, design, structure, plan, worktree, implement, PR; or research/plan/implement), each stage a fresh context producing its own artifact.

cards.claim: A standard research-plan-implement workflow makes parallel agents comparable, because every checkpoint artifact has the same shape (three research docs look alike) so check-ins do not require rebuilding context.
cards.note: Standard RPI shape makes parallel agent check-ins comparable.

label: Run multiple agents or competing plans in parallel (separate worktrees, divergent constraints) and keep or synthesise the best, via judgement or a comparing orchestrator.

cards.claim: Co-host Vaibhav runs the same task on several models in separate worktrees and merges the best pieces, finding design work benefits since no single model gets it right; Dex responds with parallel markdown drafts in different styles (not Dex's own idea).
cards.note: Co-host runs the same task on several models in worktrees and merges best pieces.
